vocabulary.definition: The long molecule made of four repeating letters (A, T, C, G) that carries the instructions for building and running a living thing.
A specific stretch of DNA that contains the instructions for one protein or trait.
One single 'letter' in the DNA code — the basic building block of a DNA strand.
A mutation where one DNA letter is swapped for a different one, like changing one word in a sentence.
A mutation where one or more extra DNA letters are added into the sequence that weren't there before.
A mutation where one or more DNA letters are removed from the sequence.
How much (or how little) a given DNA mutation changes the protein a gene builds — ranging from no change at all, to one altered amino acid, to a fully scrambled or truncated protein.
A scrambling of every instruction after an insertion or deletion, caused by shifting how the three-letter reading groups line up.
A group of three DNA (or RNA) letters that the cell reads as the instruction for one amino acid.
A working molecule built from a chain of amino acids, assembled according to a gene's instructions; proteins do most of the jobs inside a cell.
Something in the environment — like UV light, certain chemicals, or radiation — that raises the chance of a mutation occurring.
A mutation in a sperm or egg cell, which can be passed down to offspring.
A mutation in a regular body cell, which affects only that individual and is not inherited by their offspring.

structureCards.label: Substitution mutation
structureCards.function: Swaps one DNA letter (nucleotide) for a different one at a single position in the sequence, without changing the total length of the strand.
structureCards.whereItIs: Can occur anywhere along a gene; in this model, shown at the bp-6 rung within the mutation overlay segment (bp 5-7).
structureCards.whyItMatters: Because the genetic code is read in three-letter codons and several codons can code for the same amino acid, a substitution sometimes changes nothing (silent), sometimes swaps one amino acid (missense), and occasionally creates an early stop signal (nonsense) — but it never shifts the reading frame for the rest of the sequence.

structureCards.label: Insertion mutation
structureCards.function: Adds one or more extra DNA letters into the sequence that weren't there before, lengthening the strand at that point.
structureCards.whereItIs: Can occur anywhere along a gene; in this model, shown as a new rung fading in between bp-6 and bp-7 within the mutation overlay segment.
structureCards.whyItMatters: When the number of inserted letters isn't a multiple of three, every codon boundary downstream shifts (a frameshift), usually scrambling the rest of the protein — a much larger effect than a substitution's single-codon change.

structureCards.label: Deletion mutation
structureCards.function: Removes one or more DNA letters from the sequence, shortening the strand at that point.
structureCards.whereItIs: Can occur anywhere along a gene; in this model, shown as the bp-6 rung collapsing and downstream rungs closing the gap within the mutation overlay segment.
structureCards.whyItMatters: Like an insertion, a deletion that isn't a multiple of three letters causes a frameshift, scrambling every codon downstream of the deletion point — the mirror-image case to insertion, useful for comparing how both disrupt the reading frame the same way while substitution does not.

structureCards.label: Effect on protein function
structureCards.function: Compares the reference protein (built from the unmutated gene) against the protein built from whichever mutated DNA state is currently active, to show how much the final protein actually changes.
structureCards.whereItIs: Shown in the protein-readout layer below the DNA strand — two parallel amino acid bead chains (reference on top, current mutation state below) that only appear when this hotspot is opened.
structureCards.whyItMatters: This is the payoff step of the whole component: it makes visible why a one-letter DNA change can be invisible (silent substitution), small (missense substitution — one bead recolors), or dramatic (insertion/deletion — most of the downstream chain scrambles), connecting the DNA-level edit to a real functional consequence.
